ANNOUNCEMENT BY THE CHAIR 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon’ble Members, the Finance Bill, 2026, was included in today’s 
List of Business, subject to the receipt of hon’ble President’s recommendation. The 
same has since been received, and the Bill will now be taken up in the House from 
2.00 P.M. onwards.  
Hon’ble Members, against the allocated seven hours for combined discussion 
on the Appropriation (No.2) Bill, 2026, eight hours and nine minutes have already 
been consumed. In order to allow Members to speak on the Finance Bill, 2026, if the 
House agrees, additional time of three hours may be allocated for the discussion. 
Accordingly, the allocation of time to parties will be made as per 11 hours. 
Thereafter, the hon’ble Finance Minister will give a combined reply to the 
discussions on the Appropriation (No.2) Bill, 2026, and the Finance Bill, 2026.

the existing wharf, undertaking capital dredging, and acquiring land for the

operational efficiency and economic output.

training etc.

Integration of digital land records with agricultural schemes 
*364. SHRIMATI SULATA DEO: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
[ 27 March, 2026 ]
69

(a)  whether the Ministry proposes to introduce integration of digital land records 
with agricultural schemes in Odisha to ensure transparency in Direct Benefit 
Transfer (DBT); and 
(b)  if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI SHIVRAJ 
SINGH CHOUHAN): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) and (b) Yes, Odisha is utilizing digital land records of farmers for the 
purpose of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) under various agricultural schemes.  Odisha 
has operationalized the integration of digital land records, i.e., the Bhulekh database, 
with agricultural schemes in the State. The land records in the State are digitized and 
maintained by the Revenue and Disaster Management Department, Govt. of Odisha, 
in the Bhulekh portal. 
The State of Odisha has informed that the digitized land record database of the 
State is used for identification of landholding categories (such as small and marginal 
farmers) under the State Sector farmers’ welfare scheme, i.e. CM KISAN.  
Further, the State Farmers Registry under AgriStack, built using the Record of 
Rights in the sta te of Odisha covers landholding farmers, livestock and fisheries 
farmer, and provides them with a digital identity, called Farmer ID. It has been 
designed to integrate and validate farmer -related data. This helps enable accurate 
identification of eligible beneficiaries and helps enable Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) 
to the farmers with enhanced transparency, and efficient delivery of scheme benefits. 
Odisha has linked the AgriStack to register new farmers under the PM KISAN 
scheme. 
Under both CM KISAN and PM  KISAN schemes, financial assistance is 
transferred directly to the bank accounts of eligible farmers through DBT mode. 
 The State also captures digitized land record information at the time of farmer 
registration / Krushak Odisha (the State’s own farmer database) at the time of farmer 
registration. These records are subsequently used for DBT of various benefits, 
including seed input subsidy and need -based input assistance, to the farmers across 
the State.During the release of 22nd installment of PM Kisan i n Odisha, 34,18,193 
beneficiaries received benefit of scheme amounting to 683.64 cr. The total amount 
70
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

disbursed till date through DBT for the farmers in Odisha under PM -KISAN is 
Rs.14,486.34 crores. 
Further, the Digital Crop Survey, i.e., survey to digital ly capture crops being 
grown on every farmland in the country with photos and geo -tags, has enabled plot-
level visibility of crops and better estimation of areas sown across seasons, which in 
turn supports evidence-based planning for production estimation, procurement, input 
supply and logistics management. In Kharif 2025, the Digital Crop Survey (DCS) has 
been conducted in 604 Districts covering more than 28.5 crores plots, including 2.56

Shri Nara Chandrababu Naidu Garu. The Finance Bill, 2026, rests  on five principles. 
One, trust-based tax administration; two, ease of living for common citizens; three, 
empowering the MSMEs, farmers and cooperatives; four, making India a stronger 
global business hub; five, customs reform.  
 First is trust -based tax ad ministration and legal framework. With the foreign 
assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme 2026, a new chapter allows small 
taxpayers to declare small overseas assets up to Rs.5 crore or undisclosed foreign 
income upto Rs.1 crore without facing prosecu tion, providing immense relief for 
inadvertent omissions.  Now I come to decriminalization and reduction of

rationalising criminal provisions under the Income -tax framework. Then revised and 
updated returns. To facilitate compliance, taxpayers are now permitted to update or 
revise returns even after reassessment proceedings, subject to an additional ten per 
cent tax. Additionally, the time limit for revised return is extended to 12 months from 
the end of the relevant tax year. Then I come to Dispute Resolution Committee. The 
DRC empowered to waive off penalties and grant immunity from prosecution for small 
and medium taxpayers, aiming to reduce litigation.  
 Now I come to middle class and ease of living reliefs. First is collection of tax 
at source. TCS for remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) for 
education and medical purposes has been slashed from five per cent to two per cent.

completely removed. Tax Deducted at Source – A new system allows certain 
depositors to directly accept declarations like Form 15G and Form 15H and distribute 
them on behalf of senior citizens and small savers, ending the hassle of submitting 
multiple physical forms to different agencies. Exemption for disability pension, a 
statutory tax exemption, has been granted for disability pensions. Then, Amendment 
of First Schedule – Passenger allowances, tariffs on gifts and rules around personal 
imports -- have been rationalised to reduce daily disputes at airports.  Then, 
agriculture, MSMEs and cooperatives: Deduction in respect of income of cooperative 
societies – Primary cooperative societies now enjoy tax deductions not just for 
supplying milk, fruits and vegetables, but the ambit has been expanded to include 
cattle feed and cotton seed. Deduction for I nter-Cooperative Dividends – Dividend 
income received by federal cooperatives from their investments is now tax -
deductable under the new tax regime, provided it is distributed further down to its 
members. Special provision for fishing and fishing related a ctivities – Indian-flagged 
fishing vessels operating beyond India’s territorial waters can now bring harvested fish

infrastructure sector – To prevent foreign cloud providers from s etting up hollow

Need to strengthen the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) 
SHRI NIRANJAN BISHI (Odisha) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I seek to draw the 
attention of the Government towards the functioning of the National Commission for 
Scheduled Tribes (NCST), a vital constitutional body entrusted with safeguarding the 
rights and interests of our tribal communities. The NCST has been established under 
Article 338A of the C onstitution of India, with the mandate to investigate, monitor and 
evaluate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for the Scheduled Tribes. The 
Commission is vested with the powers of a Civil Court in matters of inquiry, including 
summoning witne sses, requisitioning documents, and receiving evidence on 
affidavits. As of late 2023 and early 2024, four out of five key constitutional positions in 
the NCST remain vacant — including the Chairperson (vacant since 27 June 2023), 
the Vice -Chairperson (vac ant since 2019), and two Member positions. This has 
severely affected the decision -making capacity and institutional effectiveness of the 
Commission. Further, out of a total sanctioned strength of 124 posts, over  70 
positions remain vacant, including critical posts such as Directors, Research Officers, 
Law Officers, Accounts Officers, and Superintendent of Police. The Commission is 
functioning at less than 50 per cent capacity, significantly hampering its ability to 
conduct investigations, address grievances, and ensure justice for Scheduled Tribes. 
Therefore, I urge the Government to take necessary steps to fill all vacant positions, 
strengthen institutional capacity, and empower the NCST to effectively discharge its 
constitutional responsibilities across the country.

Demand for mandatory QR codes on medicines and regulation against forced sale    
of full strips 
SHRI GOLLA BABURAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Sir, this House has expressed concern 
many times over increasing out-of-pocket expenses year-after-year on health.   
According to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, 60 
per cent of medical expenditure by outpatie nts is on medicines and 30 per cent of 
medical expenditure by inpatients is on me dicines. And, one of the reasons behind 
this is that chemists are forcing patients to buy the entire strip of tablets or capsules 
when they need only 2 or 3 tablets, or 4 or  5 tables, when prescription is only for a 
day or two or three. There were protests and dharnas on this issue. So, by 
acknowledging problems that patients face, when chemists insist on selling entire 
strip of tablets or capsules, the Government  of India held consultations with pharma 
and medical devices industry to find solution to protect the interests of patients. This 
exercise was done three years ago. During  the discussion, even the Drugs Controller 
[ 30 March, 2026 ]
15

General of India was present. But, so far,  no positive results have come. So, to 
address this problem, there are a few areas which need to be explored.  The first one 
is to find new packing technology fo r medicines. The Government can adopt 
perforation technology in medicine strips which create precise, weak tear lines 
between individual tablets or capsule unit s. This helps easy separation. But, here, 
there is a problem. The problem is, individual tablet or capsule does not contain batch 
number, manufacturing, expiry date and details of salts. So, for this purpose, the 
Government can direct the pharma and medi cal devices industry to print QR Code or 
Bar Code on all medicines, so that if the patient purchases even a single tablet or a 
blister pack, he can get the details thro ugh QR Code. This way, each individual 
segment can have details. This will in crease affordability, reduce wastage of 
medicines and enables patients to buy only as  per the prescribed course.  As of now, 
there is no nationwide uniform law forbidding the compulsory sale of full strips as well 
as for putting mandatory QR Code on each ta blet or capsule. Hence, I appeal to the 
Government of India to either formulate law or amend the Drug Rules, 1945, for this 
purpose which will go a long way in re ducing out-of-pocket-expenses thereby 
lessening financial burden on patients.

disciplinary actions against dissenting voic es have raised con cerns about shrinking 
spaces for dialogue. Universities encour age debates, seminars and student-led 
discussions without fear of censorship or  retaliation. Strengthening institutional 
autonomy and reducing undue political in terference are also essential steps in 
maintaining academic independence. Ultimately , preserving freedom of expression in 
Indian Universities requires a collectiv e effort from administrators a nd the 
Government.

 (a) to (d) The Micro and Small Enterp rises - Cluster Development Programme 
(MSE-CDP) is a Central Sector Scheme aimed at enhancing productivity and 
competitiveness of MSMEs through cluste r-based interventions. Under the scheme, 
Common Facility Centre (CFC) proposals are identified by MSME stakeholders and 
forwarded by State Governments after due examination, while Infrastructure 
Development (ID) projects are identified by State Governments and recommended 
for approval. Government grants are releas ed in phases, based on the progress of 
the projects.

which 47 projects are in Andhra Pradesh.  These include 11 Common Facility Centres 
and 36 Infrastructure Development projects. Out of 47 projects approved in Andhra 
Pradesh, 5 CFCs and 12 Infrastructure Development projects stand completed and 
are operational. As per information received from State Government, these projects 
have generated employment of approximately 8300 Nos. in CFC Projects and 57793 
Nos. in ID Projects.

from Govt. of Telangana during the last three years. 
 Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) scheme, being implemented by Department of 
Agriculture and Farmer’s Welfare, was impl emented under the umbrella of PMKSY till 
March, 2022 and now being implemented und er Pradhan Mantri - Rashtriya Krishi 
Vikash Yojna (PM-RKVY). PDMC scheme focuses on enhancing water use efficiency 
at the farm level through micro-irrigation techniques, namely drip and sprinkler 
systems. Total central assistance of Rs. 873.95 Crore has been provided to 
Telangana under PDMC, out of which, Rs. 194.63 Crore provided during the last three 
years. 
 (b)  Central Water Commission (CWC) under Department of Water 
Resources, River Development and Gang a Rejuvenation (DoWR, RD & GR) 
provides techno-economic appraisal of majo r and medium irrigation projects. This 
includes assessment of water availability, examination of inter-State aspects, 
irrigation planning, overall techno-economi c viability of the project etc. It also 
monitors projects included under ongoing schemes of DoWR, RD & GR for central 
assistance.

thunderstorms, cloudbursts and increasing climate induced extreme weather events, 
the North-East region requires a far strong er and denser weather monitoring system 
than what presently exists. Here are some  reasons for additional Doppler Weather 
Radars (DWRs) in the region. Firstly, improved forecasting and early warning -- 
Doppler Radars can accurately track precipi tation patterns, detect thunderstorms, 
and provide early warnings for floods, landslides, and cyclones. Second is, 
strengthening Disaster Management.  With better weather forecasting, authorities can 
evacuate people, prepare emergency services, and minimize damage to 
infrastructure and agriculture. Third is, agricultural benefits. Accurate weather 
forecasts can help farmers to plan their acti vities, reducing crop losses and improving 
yields. Fourth is, flood and landslide risk reduction. North East India is prone to 
floods, and Doppler Radars can help mo nitor rainfall patterns, enabling timely 
interventions. Fifth is, climate change mi tigation. As climate change increases 
extreme weather events, Doppler Radars can help to monitor and predict these 
changes. 
 Currently, there are limited Doppler Rada r installations in the North East. In 
Assam, these radars are installed at Guwa hati, Dhubri, Jorhat, Tezpur, and Silchar. 
In Mizoram at Aizawl, in Nagaland at Dimapur, in Manipur at Imphal, and in Arunachal 
Pradesh at Mandala Top and Namsai. Adding  more DWRs can significantly improve 
weather forecasting and disaster management in the region. I, therefore, urge the 
Government to set up more Doppler Weather Radars in the North East Region.

Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

the transportation of goods. Faster and smoother freight movement will support

and economic importance of this highway an d approaching monsoon, it is imperative 
that the project be completed at the earliest on a priority and time-bound basis.

stakeholders and provide a clear timeline for its early completion, especially before the

Concern over commercialization of healthcare and exploitation by  
private hospitals 
SHRI SANT BALBIR SINGH (Punjab) : & Hon’ble Chairman Sir, I thank you for giving 
me this opportunity. Sat Sri Akal to all th e Hon’ble Members present in this House. 
Sir, in our country, doctors have traditionally been accorded the status of God, and 
medical services have always been regard ed as sacred. However, it is deeply 
concerning that healthcare today is increasingly being commercialized and treated as 
a profit-making enterprise. Private hospitals have become prohibitively expensive and 
are beyond the reach of the common man. At the same time, insurance companies 
lure citizens into purchasing policies through tall claims and assurances of 
comprehensive support during medical em ergencies—moments when individuals are 
most vulnerable and in need of care. However, when claims are actually made, 
patients are often denied benefits on the basis of complex, technical, and fine-print 
terms and conditions. These clauses are de liberately drafted in a manner that is 
difficult for an ordinary person to understan d, resulting in exploitation and financial 
distress for consumers. Sir, I urge the Government to take immediate steps to 
regulate both private hospitals and insura nce companies, and to put an end to the 
exploitation of the common ma n. There is an urgent need to plug systemic loopholes 
and ensure transparency and accountability in this sector. Further, I strongly 
recommend that all policy terms and conditio ns must be written in simple language, 
preferably in the mother to ngue of the consumer, so that individuals can fully 
understand their rights and obligations and protect themselves from unfair practices. 
Sir, today, patients are increasingly being treated as mere commodities for profit, with 
private hospitals and insurance companies often acting in collusion, thereby 
compromising access to quality and a ffordable healthcare. Due to such 
circumstances, patients from nearly eight st ates are compelled to seek treatment at 
PGI Chandigarh, leading to excessive burden on the institution and immense hardship 
for patients and their families. Therefore,  I demand that another super-specialty 
hospital be established in this region of Punjab to reduce the load on PGI and improve 
accessibility to quality healthcare. It is the responsibility of the Government to ensure 
adequate medical infrastructure for its ci tizens. At the same time, I would like to 
inform this august House with a sense of pr ide that Punjab has become the first state 
to provide free medical treatment up to ₹10 lakh through empanelled hospitals. I urge 
that such a progressive scheme be replicated across other states for the benefit of the 
wider population. Thank you, Sir.

(c) the details of Central funds proactively utilized to equip ITIs in Uttar Pradesh

Statement 
 (a) and (b)  The Government has launched Pradhan Mantri Skilling and 
Employability Transformation through Up graded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme for the 
infrastructure upgradation of Industrial Tr aining Institutes (ITIs) across the country 
including the State of Uttar Pradesh. The scheme envisages to enhance the overall 
quality and relevance of vocational traini ng with upgraded labs, machines, and 
industry-aligned curriculum in the country. The Scheme has a total outlay of Rs. 
60,000 crores (Central Share – Rs. 30,00 0 crore, State Share – Rs. 20,000 crore 
and Industry Share – Rs. 10,000 crore). 
The key objectives of the scheme are: 
i. To improve the quality of training delivery in ITIs and National Skill Training      
 Institutes (NSTIs); 
ii. To modernize infrastructure and equipment as per industry standards; 
iii.  To introduce industry-aligned long-term and short-term courses, especially 
 in new and emerging sectors; 
iv.  To strengthen industry linkage for demand-driven skilling and better 
 employment outcomes; and 
v. To enhance the capacity of National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs) for  
 training of trainers. 
The scheme comprises of two components: 
Component I – Upgradation of 1,000 Government ITIs (200 Hub ITIs and 800 
Spoke ITIs) in a Hub and Spoke model wherein upgradation includes smart 
classrooms, modern labs, digital content, and new courses aligned to industry 
needs. 
Component II – Capacity Augmentation of five NSTIs located in Bhubaneswar, 
Chennai, Hyderabad, Kanpur, and Ludhiana, including setting-up sector-
specific National Centres of Excellence for skilling, with focus on advanced 
training of trainers with global partnership.

55

 
 
Under the PM-SETU scheme, industry pa rticipation in curriculum design, 
training delivery and apprenticeship opportunities is strengthened through an 
industry-led governance model. The indust ry-led Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) is 
provided the necessary autonomy to prop ose modifications in the curriculum by 
introducing new courses and upgrading existing courses as per industry 
requirements. The scheme focuses on im proving employability outcomes through 
industry-led governance and aims to enable  learners to acquire industry-relevant 
skills, gain exposure to real work environments, and access career guidance, 
placement support and self-employment opportunities through strengthened 
institutional systems and industry linkages. 
Upgradation of curricula for ITI training programmes is a continuous process 
and is generally undertaken every three ye ars. To meet the demands of the modern 
economy and emerging technologies in the industrial sector, new courses are 
continuously developed and existing cour ses are upgraded in consultation with 
industry, academia and States/UTs. The courses are updated by incorporating new 
technologies and the latest tools, equipm ent and machinery in the curricula, keeping 
in view the requirements of emerging technologies. During the last three years, 14 
Craftsmen Training Scheme (CTS) courses, 15 short-term courses and 07 Flexi-MoU 
courses have been develo ped and approved by National Council for Vocational 
Education and Training (NCVET). Addition ally, 22 courses have been revised and 
approved to further align training with in dustry requirements. The list is attached at 
Annexure-I. 
Under CTS, 31 New Age Courses, in cluding Green Hydrogen Production 
Technician and Internet of Things Technician, have been intr oduced in ITIs. The 
enrolment of trainees in ITIs across the country in the New Age Courses has increased 
from 8,611 in session 2022-23 to 42,338 in session 2025-26. The list of these 31 New 
Age Courses is at Annexure-II. 
 (c)  Release of funds under PM- SETU for Upgradation of ITIs  is contingent 
upon the formation of SPV. MSDE is carryi ng out necessary consultations to support 
and handhold States/UTs across various as pects of scheme roll-out. At present, 
proposals regarding upgradation of ITIs is yet to be received from State Steering 
Committee for consideration or approval of National Steering Committee (NSC). 
It is pertinent to mention that the Mi nistry has made significant progress in 
enabling States/UTs to move forward. 35 States/UTs have identified clusters, 32 have

formed State Steering Committees, 25 have created State Budget Heads, 19 have 
floated EOIs for AIPs, and 12 have floated RFPs for inviting interest of industry. 
 (d)   Mandatory industry linkages, includin g provisions such as On-the-Job 
Training (OJT), facilitate structured en gagement between ITIs and industry. This 
exposure enables trainees to acquire hands-on experience in real work environments, 
align their skills with industry requirem ents, and develop essential employability 
competencies such as communication, t eamwork, and work ethics. Such industry-
integrated training enhances the job-read iness of ITI graduates and improves their 
prospects for wage employment. Further, Under the PM-SETU scheme, industry-led 
Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) would l ead the upgradation and be empowered to 
propose necessary interventions relating to curriculum redesign, training delivery 
models, infrastructure upgradation and in dustry exposure, in alignment with local 
industry needs and the Scheme guidelines. 
 (e)  The Directorate General of Training (DGT) under the aegis of the 
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneur ship (MSDE) is implementing the Dual 
System of Training (DST) in ITIs under the CTS to strengthen industry linkage in skill 
training. Under DST, a substantial portion of practical training is conducted at industry 
premises, enabling trainees to gain ha nds-on experience on modern tools, 
equipment and machinery, thereby enhanc ing their employability. This enables 
industries to train candidates according to  their skill requirements while providing 
trainees with hands-on industry experience aligned with market demand. 
With effect from the academic session 20 23–24, all new affili ations granted in 
the third shift in ITIs have been made mandatory under DST mode, thereby promoting 
the adoption of DST mode acr oss ITIs. Enrolment in ITIs under DST during the last 
two sessions was 33,566 in 2024–25 and 39,136 in 2025–26 
Further, the proportion of trainees en rolled under DST relative to the total 
number of trainees in an ITI has been incorporated as a pa rameter in the Data Driven 
Grading Methodology (DDGM) for grading of  ITIs, with higher enrolment under DST 
resulting in a higher score under the said parameter. 
In addition, the Strategic Advisory and Reforms Taskforce for Holistic ITI 
Transformation (SARTHI) has been cons tituted under the chairmanship of the 
Minister of State (Independent Charge), MSDE, to provide advisory inputs on 
curriculum development and standardization, trade testing and certification reforms, 
accreditation and regulatory norms for ITIs , strengthening of industry–institute

Demand for creation of an independent Postal Circle for Goa 
SHRI SADANAND MHALU SHET TANAVADE (Goa) : Sir, I seek to draw attention of 
the Government to a serious administrative issue concerning postal administration in 
Goa. At present, postal services in Go a are administered under the Maharashtra 
Postal Circle. Despite being a separate State with its own distinct identity, Goa 
continues to remain under the administrative control of this circle. While this 
arrangement may have been suitable earlier , it no longer meets present needs, as 
Goa has its own administrative, linguistic and socio-economic requirements. This 
continued dependence on another State’s ad ministrative structure has led to several 
practical challenges. Firstly, recruitment to postal services is conducted at the circle 
level. As a result, candidates from larger  States tend to dominate the selection 
process due to greater competition, thereby limiting fair employment opportunities for 
164
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
local youth in Goa and reducing their repr esentation in public service delivery.  
Secondly, many employees recruited from ou tside Goa seek transfers back to their 
parent States after a short tenure, leadin g to recurring vacancies. These vacancies 
are often managed through temporary arrangements, affecting continuity and 
efficiency in postal services. Goa’s small ge ographical size should not be seen as a 
constraint, but rather as an advantage in  creating a more responsive, efficient and 
citizen-centric postal administration. 
I, therefore, urge the Government to co nsider the creation of an independent 
postal circle for Goa. This step will ensu re better administrative control, improve 
service delivery and enhance employment opportunities for local youth in Goa.

Concerns regarding unfair rejection and delay in health insurance claim  
settlements by private insurance companies 
DR. MEDHA VISHRAM KULKARNI (Maharashtra): Sir, I seek to draw the attention of 
the Government to the growing concern re garding the increasing instances of delay 
and unjust rejection of health insuran ce claims by certain private insurance 
companies, causing serious hardship to policyholders across the country. Private 
insurers promote health policies with pr omises of cashless treatment and quick 
settlement of claims. Yet, during medical emergencies many families later find their 
claims partially approved, delayed, or re jected on technical grounds such as pre-
existing disease clauses, documentation issues, or restrictive policy conditions. 
According to the latest annual report of the Insurance Regulatory and Development 
Authority of India, nearly 2.57 lakh complain ts were registered in the insurance sector 
during 2024-25, including about 1.22 lakh related to claim settlement disputes, a large 
share from health insurance. Policyholders have also raised concerns regarding the 
practices of certain insurers where de lays, repeated document requests and 
prolonged verification processes create difficult ies for patients and hospitals. In many

cases, patients enter hospitals expecting insurance coverage, but at the time of 
discharge, families have to arrange large payments due to unresolved claims, placing 
severe financial and emotional pressure on ordinary citizens. 
I, therefore, urge the Government to strengthen regulatory oversight, ensure 
strict action against insurers unfairly rejecting claims, mandate dedicated claim-
settlement managers to coordinate with hosp itals, require transparent disclosure of 
policy terms before sale and ensure that a ll insurance-related complaints are resolved 
within a fixed time frame of 30 days to protect policyholders and maintain public 
confidence in the health insurance system.

REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
 World Autism Awareness Day 
MR. CHAIRMAN :  Hon’ble Members, today, April 2 is observed globally as World 
Autism Awareness Day, as designated by the United Nations.  On this occasion, this 
House reiterates its commitment to safeguarding the rights and promoting the welfare 
of persons with autism. 
The United Nations theme for this year,  “Advancing Neurodiversity and the UN 
Sustainable Development Goals ”, emphasizes the need to recognize neurodiversity 
as an integral part of human diversity and to ensure that our developmental efforts are 
inclusive and sustainable. Autism Spec trum Disorder affects communication, 
behaviour and social interaction; howe ver, individuals on the spectrum possess 
distinctive strengths and capabilities which, with appropriate support and 
opportunities, can greatly enrich our society. 
India has put in place a robust legisl ative framework through the Rights of 
Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and the National Trust Act, 1999, to secure rights 
and extend necessary support services. Nevertheless, laws and schemes achieve 
their true purpose only when their benefits reach every eligible is individual. Greater 
focus on early diagnosis, inclusive educat ion, skill training and awareness at the 
community level is essential to bridge existing gaps and promote equality.

determination to foster an environment of understanding, acceptance and equal 
participation. An inclusive society is streng thened when every citizen, irrespective of 
ability, is given the opportunity to contribute and succeed.  It our shared responsibility 
to ensure that persons with autism are not merely accommodated, but fully 
empowered as valued members of our national community.

MATTERS RAISED WITH PERMISSION  
Need for expedited completion of Kawrpui River Bridge Project under India-
Bangladesh Agreement  
SHRI K. VANLALVENA (Mizoram) :  Sir, I rise today with deep gratitude to mention 
the ongoing construction of a bridge over th e Khawthlang Tuipui river, undertaken by 
the Ministry of Home Affairs. During my visi t to several Border Outposts of the Border 
Security Force along the Indo-Bangladesh border in Mizoram in 2021, I witnessed 
first-hand the immense challenges faced by our jawans and the local villagers. Many 
BOPs had no road connectivity due to abse nce of a bridge across the Khawthlang 
Tuipui river. Likewise, several villages in this border areas remained completely cut off 
from the rest of the country.  The officers of the BSF and the leaders of these villages 
shared with me their difficulties, especially during the rainy season when floods isolate 
the region for days. Tragically, innocent ch ildren have lost their lives because medical 
help could not reach them in time due to lack of roads and bridges. Moved by their 
16
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
plight, I submitted a request to the hon’bl e Union Home Minister for sanctioning the 
construction of a bridge near  Tlabung village over the Khaw thlang Tuipui river. I am 
grateful that the Ministry of Home Affairs approved this request and sanctioned Rs. 54 
crores for the project. The construction has now begun and is expected to be 
completed within two years.  Once completed, this bridge will be a lifeline for the poor 
and marginalized people living in these re mote border areas. It will connect them to 
the rest of Mizoram, open access to essent ial services, and improve their daily lives. 
At the same time, it will greatly assist our soldiers in ensuring security and in carrying 
out their duties more effectively. Hon’ble Chairman, Sir, I place on record my heartfelt 
thanks to the hon’ble  Home Minister, Shri Amit Shah, for this generous and timely 
intervention in favour of Mizoram. This brid ge will stand as a lasting testament to the 
Government's commitment to both national  security and welfare of our border 
communities.  In the meantime, it is pertinent to recall that a bilateral agreement for 
establishing a Border Trade Centre at  Kawrpuichhuah was signed between the 
Governments of India and Bangladesh over ten years ago.  As per the agreement, a 
new bridge was to be constructed across the Kawnpui River to connect the two 
countries and facilitate trade and cooperation.  However, despite the passage of a 
decade since the signing of this agreement,  no concrete steps have been taken to 
implement the project, leaving the commitment  unfulfilled to this day. Therefore, I 
humbly request the Union Government to  initiate without further delay the 
construction of the proposed bridge acr oss the Kawnpui River, along with all 
necessary supporting infrastructure, as envisaged under the agreement signed with 
the Bangladesh Government.  Timely action on this matter will not only honour the 
commitment made over a decade ago but also strengthen bilateral trade, connectivity 
and cooperation between the two nations.

Concern over shortfall in transfer of cess collections to designated funds 
SHRI A. D. SINGH (Bihar) : Sir, the Comptroller and Au ditor General has revealed 
that as of 2023-24, the Central Government failed to transfer Rs. 3.69 lakh crore 
worth of such collection to the designated funds for which they were levied. These 
shortfalls span several decades, beginning in 1974 and continue to more recent years. 
The largest shortfall relates to Oil Indu stry Development Board, wherein between 
1974-75 and 1991-92, an amount of Rs . 902.40 crore was transferred but, 
subsequently, amounts were not fully transfe rred, leaving a total shortfall of Rs. 2.95 
crore up to the financial year 2023-24.  An other major area of shortfall was the Health 
and Education Cess. The levy was not fully transferred to the designated funds.  
The CAG reported that between 2018-19 and 2023-24, the Centre did not 
transfer Rs.37,537 crore.  Other funds impacted include the Investor Education and 
Protection Fund (Rs.2,505.5 crore) and the Monetisation of National Highways Fund 
(Rs.5,968.1 crore).  While the Finance Mini stry claimed that Rs.3.66 lakh crore had 
been transferred between 2018-19 and 2023-24, the CAG stressed the need for 
reconciliation since the Government accounts reflected only Rs.2.65 lakh crore.  The 
findings highlight persistent lapses in channeling cess proceeds towards their 
intended developmental purposes.  The pe ople of this country are entitled to 
transparency and assurance that their contri butions through cesses are utilized solely 
for the intended developmental and welfare objectives.  This House should know as 
to why cess collections were not duly transferred to the designated funds and what 
immediate steps the Government has taken to ensure that cess proceeds are 
allocated to their rightful purposes.

Coverage of National Mission for Green India 
#*406.  SHRI CHUNNILAL GARASIYA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT, FOREST 
AND CLIMATE CHANGE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is aware of decline in tree plantation activities 
recorded under the National Mission for Green India during the period 
between 2015 and 2025; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by the Ministry to address the shortfalls and 
accelerate plantation activities under the Mission; 
(c) the specific role of the weightage given by the 16th Finance Commission in 
encouraging States to increase their forest cover; 
(d) whether the Ministry has successfully integrated carbon sequestration 
monitoring into the design of the Mission; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof?

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND 
CLIMATE CHANGE   (SHRI KIRTIVARDHAN SINGH) : (a) to (e) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b)  The National Mission for a Green India (NMGI) is one of the nine 
Missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) and aims to 
protect, restore and enhance forest and tree cover while contributing to climate 
change mitigation and adaptation through plantation and ecosystem restoration in 
identified landscapes. The Green India Mi ssion (GIM), a scheme under the NMGI, 
adopts a landscape-based approach, wh erein interventions are planned and 
implemented across contiguous forest and non-forest areas, integrating ecological, 
hydrological, and socio-economic dimensio ns. Activities under GIM are undertaken 
based on approved Perspective Plans an d Annual Plans of Operation (APOs) 
submitted by States/UTs and approved by the National Executive Council. The 
Mission is implemented through a conv ergence-based framework, leveraging 
resources from various Central and State Government schemes and programmes.  
GIM being a long-term mission focused on ecosystem restoration, 
afforestation, and climate adaptation, plantation and eco-restoration activities under 
GIM may vary across the years due to factor s such as phased approvals of plans, 
timely availability of funds, and institutional preparedness at the State level. GIM has 
contributed to the overall increase in India’s forest and tree cover. As per the India 
State of Forest Report (ISFR), forest and tree cover has increased from 7,94,245 sq 
km in 2015 to 8,27,356.95 sq km in 2023, registering a net increase of 33,111.95 sq 
km. These gains are attributable to sustained afforestation and eco-restoration efforts 
undertaken through coordinated actions of Central and State Governments under 
various schemes, including GIM.  
Further, under the overarching theme of “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam”, a nationwide 
voluntary plantation initiative was launched on 5th June 2024 to promote tree planting 
through public participation and convergence with ongoing schemes. 
To address gaps and accelerate implementation, the Ministry has taken several 
measures, including; Strengthening planni ng processes with improved technical 
support; Promoting convergence with Central and State schemes and programmes of 
line departments; Streamlining fund flow  mechanisms and enhancing transparency 
38
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
through digital monitoring t ools; and Encouraging adoption  of site-specific, climate-
resilient plantation models.     
(c) The 16th Finance Commission has been mandated to recommend the 
distribution of central taxes among States taking into account several factors 
including forest cover. The Commission in its report has relied upon the framework 
that uses forest and tree cover data (as per India State of Forest Reports), including 
Very Dense, Moderately Dense and Open Forest categories, for incentivizing States. 
This approach aligns fiscal devolution with  national priorities and provides financial 
resources to States to support afforestation, ecological restoration, and sustainable 
forest management, complementing initiatives like the Green India Mission. 
(d) and (e) Monitoring of forest and tree cover, including assessment of forest 
carbon stock, is carried out biennially by the Forest Survey of India (FSI)  using 
remote sensing, GIS-based tools, and ground-based inventory methods. These 
assessments capture the impact of afforestation and restoration activities undertaken 
under various schemes, includ ing GIM. Further, the Ministry promotes the use of 
technology-based monitoring tools , including geo-tagging, remote sensing, and 
field-based verification, to improve accuracy of plantation monitoring.

Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, during the last three ye ars, the Government of India has taken 
several steps to promote biodiversity awareness in the various States and UTs 
including Uttar Pradesh through implementati on of Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (as 
amended in 2023). The Act provides for development of national and state level 
strategies and plans for conservation, promotion and sustainable use of biological 
diversity. These include measures for identi fication and monitoring of areas rich in 
biological resources, promotion of in-situ, and ex-situ, conservation of biological 
resources, including cultivars, folk variet ies and landraces, incentives for research, 
training and public education to  increase awareness with respect to biodiversity. 
         Biodiversity awareness is prom oted through a decentralized and participatory 
three-tier institutional mechanism comprisi ng the National Biod iversity Authority 
(NBA) at national level, and State Biodiver sity Boards/ Union Territory Biodiversity 
Councils at State/ UT level and Biodiversity Management Committees at grassroot 
level, ensuring effective outreach and community involvement. NBA in coordination 
with SBBs/ UTBCs facilitated the constitution of Biodiversity Management 
Committees across the Country, which play a key role in grassroot-level awareness 
and conservation activities, along with preparation of People’s Biodiversity Registers 
(PBRs) at local level to document biodiver sity and associated traditional knowledge, 
thereby enhancing awareness and community participation. 
         Pursuant to the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (as amended in 2023), the 
Biological Diversity (Access to Biological Resources and Knowledge Associated 
thereto and Fair and Equitable Sharing of Be nefits) Regulations, 2025 was notified on 
29 April 2025, superseding the Access and Benefit Sharing guidelines 2014.  As on 
date, National Biodiversity Authority coll ected Access and Benefit Sharing amount to 
the tune of Rs. 263.00 Crores, of which Rs. 145 Crores have been disbursed through 
the State Biodiversity Boards/Union Territory  Biodiversity Councils to the farmers, 
Biodiversity Management Committees and other benefit claimers. The benefit-sharing 
amount is utilized for supporting conservation activities and promoting socio-
economic development in the areas from wh ere the biological resources have been 
accessed.

the national and State/ UT levels by organizing various outreach activities for students

through training and capacity building pr ogrammes for various stakeholders including 
BMCs and Panchayat f unctionaries. BMCs have been constituted in the State at 
grassroots level. In addition, the Forest Department of Uttar Pradesh, undertook a

SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether the Ministry is undertakin g assessment and monitoring of marine 
living resources in India's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and if so, the 
details thereof;  
(b)  the number of scientific surveys conducted during the last three years for 
estimation of fishery resources and marine biodiversity; 
(c) whether the data generated through these surveys are being used to 
support sustainable fisheries management and marine conservation and if

(d) the steps taken by the Ministry to  strengthen scientific research and 
monitoring of marine ecosystems in Indian waters? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH SCIENCES (DR. JITENDRA 
SINGH): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) Yes Sir. The Centre for Marine Li ving Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), 
an attached office of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, has been established with the 
primary mandate of assessment and monitoring  of marine living resources in India’s 
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and for deve loping management strategies for their 
conservation. The programmes under which this work is being undertaken are as 
follows: 
i. Marine Living Resources (MLR) Prog ramme of CMLRE for survey, assessment 
and monitoring of marine living resources in the Indian EEZ.  
ii. Deep Ocean Mission (DOM), under which CMLRE is the nodal agency for 
exploration and conservation of deep -sea biodiversity in India’s EEZ, 
particularly in biodiversity hotspots such as seamounts.  
iii. In addition, ICAR-Central Marine Fi sheries Research Institute (ICAR-CMFRI), 
Kochi is also conducting comprehensive and continuous programmes for 
assessment and monitoring of marine living resources across India’s territorial 
waters and EEZ. The assessment and monitoring framework operated by 
ICAR-CMFRI rests on two distinct but complementary pillars: 
[ 02 April, 2026 ]
61

 
 
(a) Landings based Production Monitoring 
(b) Life History Traits based Stock Assessment 
(b) A total of 22 research cruises were conducted during the last three 
years for estimation of fishery-resource- related parameters an d marine resource 
assessment. 17 research cruises were undertaken in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian 
Sea, 1 cruise was taken in the Indian Ocean region and 2 cruises each were 
undertaken in the Lakshadweep and Andama n seas respectively. These scientific 
cruises were done for mapping the living and fisheries resource assessment. In 
addition, the Fisheries Survey of India (FSI) and ICAR-CMFRI conduct annual stock 
assessment surveys and provide national status reports such as National Stock 
assessment (2022) and the Indian Ocean T una Commission (IOTC) linked fisheries 
data submissions (2023-24). 
(c) Yes Sir. The data generated through these surveys are being utilized for 
fishery resource and habitat assessment, id entification of biodiversity hotspots and 
spawning periods/breeding grounds of fi sh species, ecosystem studies including 
ocean acidification, and development of biodiversity/genetic databases, thereby 
supporting sustainable fisheries management and marine conservation. Further, the 
Marine Living Resources programme of CM LRE incorporates advanced technologies 
and multidisciplinary approaches, thereby improving monitoring systems and enabling 
better assessment of ocean health. Thes e efforts support evidence-based decision-
making for conservation and sustainable use of marine resources. CMLRE employs 
advanced and innovative biodiversity assessment techniques, including environmental 
DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding and genomic analyses, alongside conventional 
sampling methods. These approaches enab le both qualitative and quantitative 
assessments of biodiversity. 
(d) The steps taken by the Ministry to strengthen scientific research 
includes implementation of the Deep Ocean Mission for deep-sea biodiversity 
exploration and conservation including: 
i. Use of the FORV Sagar Sampada fo r multidisciplinary marine research 
ii. Strengthening of ocean observation syst ems through glider missions, drifters   
and Argo floats deployments 
iii. Augmentation of marine biodiversi ty databases through IndOBIS and related 
scientific capacity-building efforts.

In addition, ‘Bhavasagara’ is a designat ed national-level Marine Biodiversity 
Referral Centre established at CMLRE, Kochi. It acts as a repository for deep-sea 
faunal collections from the Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). At present, the 
repository houses a total of 3,560 voucher specimens, of which more than 70% 
represent deep-water and open-ocean species.

SHRI GOLLA BABURAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Madam Vice-Chairperson. I rise to 
speak on the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2026. It is a significant 
step towards reforming our regulatory legal framework. At its core, the Bill seeks to 
replace the culture of criminalization for minor offences with one rooted in trust and 
ease of compliance. It reflects an important shift in governance, where the aim is to 
balance enforcement with the needs of a modern growing economy.  Having said 
this, I would first like to speak about its achievements. As decriminalization reduces 
fear and unlocks economic activity, the key positive of the Jan Vishwas Bill, 2026, is 
the large-scale decriminalization of minor technical offences. By removing the threat 
of imprisonment for procedural lapses, such as filing delays or documentation errors, 
the Bill creates a more enabling enviro nment for business, especially MSMEs and

start-ups. Entrepreneurs are more likely to  take risks and expand operations when 
compliance mistakes no longer carry criminal consequences. The shift from a 
punishment-based to a trust-based regu latory framework improves investor 
sentiment, encourages formalization of enterprises, and aligns India's legal 
architecture with global best practices in business regulation and economic 
governance. It also reduces litigation and enables faster dispute resolution. 
The Bill significantly eases the burden on  India's already overburdened judicial 
system by shifting minor offences from crim inal courts to administrative adjudication. 
Instead of lengthy trials, such cases can no w be resolved through designated officers 
and monetary penalties. It also allows courts to focus on serious criminal matters 
rather than routine compliance violations.  In a country like India, where 4.87 crore 
cases are currently pending, of which about 18 per cent have been pending for over 
10 years and nearly 20 per cent between 5 to 10 years, this reform is particularly 
significant. It strengthens institutional capacity, enhances regulatory clarity, and 
contributes to a more predictable an d time-bound enforcement ecosystem.  
However, some concerns re main. While the Bill seeks to decriminalize several 
offences by replacing impris onment with civil penalties, in some cases the penalty 
amounts remain unchanged and outdated. For instance, under the NDMC Act, 1994, 
fines ranging from ₹25 to ₹100 have been retained at the same level despite being 
introduced over three decades ago.  Unrevi sed penalties may, therefore, weaken the 
overall deterrence. Similarly, offences such as failure to give notice of transfer of 
property and failure to disclose liability co ntinue with unchanged civil penalties under 
the Bill. In other instances, the Bill neithe r decriminalises the of fence nor revises the 
fine. For example, interference with a muni cipal drain under the NDMC Act, 1994, still 
carries a fine of ₹50, and has been unchanged since 1994.  There is a need for a 
standardised framework to ensu re consistency in penalties . The most important is, 
there is a risk of increased administrative discretion; and, hence, there is a need for 
safeguards. This makes it essential to build strong safeguards into the system. Clear 
guidelines, transparent procedures, and effective appellate mechanisms are 
necessary to ensure fairness and accounta bility. Without such protections, the 
intended benefits of efficiency and ease of compliance may be undermined by 
uncertainty and misuse.

community of Jammu and Kashmir 
SHRI GULAM ALI (Nominated) :  Sir, the Gujjar-Bakarwal community is a traditional 
pastoral group whose primary livelihood  depends on rearing sheep and goats. 
Livestock forms the backbone of their economy and sustenance. Therefore,

productivity, commercialization and inco me of livestock-dependent communities. 
However, despite their relevance, the Gu jjar-Bakarwal community has largely been 
unable to access these benefits, particularly  in the Jammu division. District targets

often ignored or delayed. Under the Public Good category of 525 units, not a single

representation, strengthen livelihoods, re duce marginalization, improve trust in 
institutions and enable the community to fu lly participate in development initiatives 
and national growth processes effectively and sustainably going forward ahead. I urge

SHRI YERRAM VENKATA SUBBA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh):  Sir, Andhra Pradesh 
accounts for about 22 per cent of India’s total tobacco production, making it one of 
the largest producing States in the country. Tobacco farmers in districts such as

regulatory changes affecting the legal tobacco market. Thousands of small and

be safeguarded. Many farmers have limited access to viable alternative crops due to 
soil suitability, established credit linkages and existing market infrastructure. Abrupt 
market contraction without transition support risks pushing farmers into indebtedness

support mechanism, including price stabil ization measures, credit restructuring 
assistance, export facilitation and a phased crop diversification programme with 
assured market linkage. A balanced approach  is essential to protect rural livelihoods

profile.  There is no mandatory identity ve rification, no accountability of platforms and 
no real-time fraud detection.  These companies earn crores in profit, but when fraud 
happens, they simply say “Use our site at your own risk.”  If we do not act now, these 
platforms will become hunting grounds for criminals.  I, therefore, demand the 
following from the Government : (i) Mandatory KYC verification for all users of 
matrimonial and dating sites. (ii) Legal liabil ity of platforms in case of fraud. (iii) AI-

these sites seeking trust and companionship, and rightfully so.  They must not leave 
with trauma and loss.  The time for stronger safeguards is now.  I urge the 
Government to look into this.

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of 
Shrimati Mohsina Kidwai, a former Member of this House, on the 8th of April, 2026, at 
the age of 94 years. She served as the Member of Rajya Sabha representing the State 
of Chhattisgarh for two terms, from 2004 to 2010 and from 2010 to 2016.  
Born on 1st January, 1932 in Banda District of Uttar Pradesh, Shrimati Mohsina 
Kidwai, entered public life at a young age and had a distinguished political career 
spanning over six decades. Over the cour se of her illustrious career, she had the 
distinction of serving in four different le gislatures-both the Houses of Uttar Pradesh 
Legislature and the Houses of Par liament.  Shrimati Mohsina Kidwai also served as a 
Minister in the Government of Uttar Prad esh and as Union Minister holding several 
portfolios. She made significant contribution s to public life and for the upliftment of 
weaker sections of society.  
In her passing away, the nation has lost a veteran legislator, an able 
administrator and a distinguished parliamentarian. 
Hon. Members, with profound grief, I refe r to the passing away of          
Shrimati Asha Bhonsle, one of the most iconic and versatile playback singers of India, 
on the 12th of April, 2026, at the age of 92 years. Born on 8th September, 1933, at 
Sangli in Maharashtra, Shrimati Asha Bhonsle carved an unparalleled niche for herself 
in the world of music and cinema.  With a career spanning over eight decades, she 
lent her melodious voice to thousands of so ngs in multiple Indian languages, leaving 
an indelible mark on the soundscape of Indian music.   
In recognition of her immense contribu tion to the field of music, she was 
honoured with several presti gious awards, including the  Padma 
Vibhushan, Dadasaheb Phalke  Award and National Film Award, in addition to 
numerous national and international accolade s.  She remained an inspiration to 
aspiring artists and a symbol of dedication, excellence and artistic brilliance. 
In her sad demise, the nation has lost a legendary voice, an unparalleled artist 
and a cultural icon whose legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.  We 
deeply mourn the passing away of Shrima ti Mohsina Kidwai and Shrimati Asha 
Bhosle.

REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
Achieving of first critic
ality by India’s 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor           
at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu 
MRCHAIRMAN: Hon. Members,  I would like to inform this august House of a 
significant milestone in India’s journey of scientific progress and technological self-
reliance.  On 6th April 2026, at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu, India achieved an important 
scientific breakthrough. Our 500-Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) 
has successfully attained first criticality. This marks the moment when a controlled 
and sustained nuclear chain reaction has been initiated in the reactor. 
Hon. Members, this is not merely a technological milestone; it is a moment of 
national achievement.   Over two decades  in the making, it marks the successful 
culmination of sustained efforts by thousand s of our scientists, engineers, industries 
and multiple units of the Department of At omic Energy.  This historic achievement 
bolsters the Nuclear Energy Mission and streng thens India’s global commitment of 
achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, as a nnounced by the hon. Prime Minister, 
Shri Narendra Modi ji.  The core-loading  of PFBR was also witnessed by the hon. 
Prime Minister in March 2024. 
India’s nuclear strategy is envisioned in three stages to optimise the use of our 
limited Uranium resources and abundant Thor ium reserves.  The first stage currently 
in operation uses natural Uranium in Pr essurised Heavy Water Reactors, producing 
Plutonium as a by-product.   With the real isation of PFBR, India has taken historic 
step of advancing to the second stage. In this second stage, we will utilise Plutonium 
in Fast Breeder Reactors to generate more nuclear fuel. Unlike conventional reactors, 
a Fast Breeder Reactor has the unique capa bility to produce more fuel than it 
[ 16 April, 2026 ]
3

 
 
 
 
consumes. The third stage will be Thorium-Uranium based reactors, enabling a 
sustainable, long-term energy future. 
At a time when India’s energy needs ar e steadily rising and our commitment to 
clean energy is stronger than ever, nuclear  power offers a reliable, round-the-clock, 
low-carbon source of electricity. The House had passed Sustainable Harnessing and 
Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act in December, 
2025 to open up the civil nuclear energy sector to all players. With the whole-of-the-
nation approach, we are steadily marching towards achieving the target of 100 Giga 
Watts of nuclear power.       
 With PFBR attaining criticality, India has entered the second stage of our long-
envisioned programme in civil nuclear ener gy. The PFBR stands as a proud 
testament to India’s long journey of perseverance, innovation and national 
commitment. It serves as a vital bridge, lin king our present capabilities with a more 
sustainable and Atmanirbhar nuclear future.  
This achievement has been made possibl e entirely through indigenous effort. 
The reactor has been designed by the Indi ra Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research 
(IGCAR) and constructed by Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), 
with strong participation from Indian indust ry. It stands as a proud reflection of the 
strength of our scientific ecosystem and the power of national collaboration.  
Hon. Members, with this milestone, India takes its rightful place among a 
select group of nations that have mastered this advanced technology. It reaffirms our 
standing as a nation capable of develo ping and deploying complex, frontier 
technologies with confidence and self-relian ce.  More importantly, it reflects the 
confidence of a nation that believes in its own capabilities and is determined to build a 
future that is secure, sustainable, and self-reliant.  
Looking ahead, the successful operation of PFBR will support the expansion of 
nuclear power in the country and help us move faster towards the third stage of our 
programme. It will also open new opportunities in advanced reactor technologies, fuel 
cycle systems, and high-end engineering.  
Hon. Members, this achievement marks a new beginning -- a beginning that 
carries forward the vision of our pioneers in  science; a beginning that strengthens our 
4
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
 
 
journey towards energy independence and a be ginning that brings us closer to the 
goal of a Viksit Bharat .   It is also a moment that reaffirms our belief in the power of 
science and technology to shape our co llective future and realise our shared 
aspirations.  
From the first spark of a controlled chain reaction in PFBR emerges not only 
energy, but also the promise of a brighter fu ture for generations to come.  I take this 
opportunity to place on record the appreci ation of this House for the scientists, 
engineers, technicians, industry partners and all stakeholders whose dedication and 
hard work have made this achievement possible.  Thank you.
